output.headline: Nick Clegg makes the case for a calmer AI debate: transparency and ‘tramlines’, not extinction talk
output.standfirst:
Former deputy PM now involved in tech industry urges focus on known threats such as cybersecurity, saying many in the sector are ‘winding themselves up into a lather’ over fears ‘godlike’ AI could exterminate humanity

  • UK politics live – latest updates
output.bodyHtml:
Nick Clegg has urged tech bosses to concentrate on the specific, known risks of AI rather than its “godlike power to exterminate humanity”, dismissing such fears as a sign that they are “breathing their own fumes”.

Cybersecurity and bioweapons are the known, specific threats that tech bosses should be addressing, the former UK deputy prime minister said, rather than the “slightly hand-wavy view that this technology is unavoidably going to develop some godlike power which is going to turn on us and exterminate humanity”.

He told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “I think it is perhaps accidentally self-serving, because it sort of implies that we can only be made safe by having everything controlled, in effect, by an oligopoly of a small number of companies, and I think it slightly paralyses the political debate.”

Clegg said he spent “a huge amount of time” with people in the tech industry. He was formerly the president of global affairs at Meta, owns more than 917,000 shares in Nscale, a UK-based datacentre, and is a cofounder of the AI startup AMI Labs.

He noted that one person who runs an AI lab said the current discourse was “totally silly”. “They don’t agree amongst themselves at all. Of course, we hear the most apocalyptic voices,” he said.

He said: “There is a culture in Silicon Valley – it’s an odd place for those who haven’t been there. It is in many ways the centre of the universe, or at least claiming to shape it. It’s also an oddly parochial place. It’s a strange sort of culture where the engineers can get quite close to the technology and start slightly breathing their own fumes as they wind themselves up into a lather about these things.”

Clegg said there was a case for “tramlines and greater transparency” when asked about the autonomous hack conducted by a group of OpenAI agents on a major real-world company, Hugging Face.

He said, however, that this would be unlikely to happen under a Trump administration given its competitiveness on AI, and he suspected China’s cooperation would be limited, since the development of AI technologies was viewed as a “national mission” after the country was “cheated out of the Industrial Revolution”.

There was, he added, room for others to work together: “I think there’s a great potential for the big three techno democracies in the world – India, Europe and the US – to collaborate more.”

Clegg urged realism when asked whether the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, could take a lead on such efforts, noting the UK was not a world leader on AI: “We need to be realistic about what influence we can and cannot exert.”

Clegg also set out why he disagreed with other proposed remedies, such as introducing a “kill switch”, which he said would be unworkable; or only producing closed models, where source code is not made public, which he said were no safer than open source models according to the evidence.

What he proposed instead was openness: “There is a lot that can be done both voluntarily and through regulation, to enforce far greater transparency on the way in which these models are concocted and how they operate.”
